paragraphs.text: "And here she is, the birthday girl, Allyzooba!" the DJ announced.
The crowd cheered as Ally entered the large ballroom. "Thank you all for coming to my party!" She twirled around, showing off her new outfit.
"Happy birthday!" everyone cried.
But from somewhere in the back of the room, a voice called, "Allyzooba!"
Ally kept twirling.
"Allyzooba!" the voice said more sharply.
Ally's eyes flew open, abruptly ending her daydream.

"Allyzooba Delta5X of Astralia!" her father called from the main control room. Her family's spaceship was docked on planet Dorpio10 for her parents' latest peace mission. As Astralians with Astral minds, they flew all over the universe. They solved major problems like severe droughts, food shortages, even wars between galaxies.
"We're back," Ally's dad called. "Our mission was a success, so we'll be taking off for home soon."
"Okay!" Ally called back. She threw her voice so it would sound as if it were coming from another part of the ship. "I'm just finishing up my homework!"
Ally picked up her tablet and continued planning her party. "Dad won't come looking for me if he thinks I'm doing homework," she thought.

But seconds later her father burst into her sleep quarters. "Homework, huh?" Dad took Ally's tablet from her. "You should watch what you think, daughter. You're not the only Astralian who can read minds."
Ally sighed. "I was hoping you were too far away."

"I was close enough for you to throw your voice to trick me. So I was close enough to read your mind." He sat beside her, his expression softening. "Mom and I are happy that you've mastered throwing your voice, and your levitation skills are improving. But you're past the age when most Astralians start going on solo missions. You need to focus on your studies to prepare."
Ally nodded. "Okay. Can I have my tablet back now?"
"I'm afraid not. Our Astral minds are revered all over the universe because we use them to help others, not plan parties."
"But parties make people happy, Dad! Doesn't that count?"
"Not as much as keeping the universe in peaceful balance," Dad said. "Your mother and I have made up our minds. It's time for you to be more responsible."
"Fine." Ally sighed. "Send me to planet GrayZone. I can teach those dull GrayZoners to be more colorful, like me!"
Ally's mom joined them. "We're going to start with a simpler task. The communication device in escape pod Alpha needs repair. Fixing it is a skill you'll need when you start going on solo missions."
Escape pods were kept on Astralians' mother ships in case things got dangerous and a quick getaway was required.
Ally moaned. "Repairs are boring."
Mom folded her arms and stared at her.
Ally didn't need to read her mind to know she would never win this argument. "Fine. I'll fix the comm device." She walked to her closet. "I'll change out of my pajamas and then get started."
A few minutes later, Ally emerged in a brightly colored outfit. She wore her favorite boots, which made her feet look especially big.
"That's your idea of work clothes?" Ally's mother asked.
Ally twirled around. "Isn't this a cute outfit?"
Her mother sighed. "It's not very practical."
"It's fine for you to wear a boring old uniform, Mom, but I have to express my personality. It's what I'm known for!"

"We want you to be known for doing good works throughout the universe," Mom said. "When we were your age, we had already been on solo missions." She held out a tablet. "Here's the manual for fixing the comm device. Take a look and let me know if you have any questions."
Ally pretended to read through it for a moment. "It seems simple enough."
Mom frowned. "You know how to check the meters? And make sure you unplug the—"

"I know all that stuff!" Ally rolled her eyes and flipped her tentacles. "See you later." As she walked to the area on the ship where the pods were stored, Ally forced herself to think about homework. She didn't want her parents detecting her real thoughts right now.

But as soon as she was out of range, those thoughts came spilling out. "I can't believe they don't trust me with something as simple as fixing a comm device. I'll show them they're wrong. I am totally ready for real Astralian missions!"
Ally intended to start working right away. But after she stepped into escape pod Alpha , she quickly got distracted.

"I haven't been in this pod in so long!" It had a comfortable sleeping unit, along with some fun entertainment options. But when she looked at the meal-o-matic that dispensed food, she saw it was nearly empty. "Looks like the food supply is running low. I'd better remind Mom to refill it when I'm done."
Ally grabbed one of the last bottles of juba juice from the machine and took a swig.
"Ahh! Still bubbly!" She turned the repair manual on and got ready to work, but there was something bothering her.
"It's too quiet in here," she murmured. She pressed a button on the dashboard and the pod's computer instantly lit up.
"Alpha," Ally commanded. "Play some fun music."
An upbeat song filled the pod.
"Satisfactory choice?" the computer asked.
"Yes! I love this song!" Ally jumped up to dance around.
When the song ended, she sighed. "I guess it's time to get to work."
"It's long past time," the computer said.
Ally scowled. "Are you going to start nagging me too? Besides, if you're so smart, why can't you fix the comm device yourself?"
"Repair of communication devices is beyond my capabilities." The computer's lights dimmed as it put itself to sleep.
"That's fine," Ally mumbled. "I don't need your help or anyone else's. I'll have this comm device working in no time." She took another sip of juba juice and sat down to work.

A short while later, Ally had taken the comm device apart, and all the pieces sat in front of her. She pushed her tentacles out of her face. "That wasn't very hard. And I found the problem. The fuse was blown. Now all I have to do is put the device back together."
The computer lit up. "Be sure to consult the manual before reassembling comm device."
"Thanks, Alpha ," Ally replied, "but I took it apart, so I can totally put it back together." She snorted. "My parents will be sorry they called me irresponsible."
The computer made a noise that sounded like "Hmm."
Before long, Ally had finished reassembling the device. "See, Alpha ?" She proudly flipped her tentacles. "I told you I didn't need the manual."
"Standing by for test of communication device," the computer said.
"Here we go!" Ally turned the device on, expecting it to light up. But nothing happened. She tried again. Still nothing.
"That's funny," Ally murmured. "I don't know what's wrong."
"Scanning area." The computer clicked and clacked. "Detecting nanochip receiver on the floor. Repeat, detecting nanochip—"
"I heard you the first time!" Ally checked the floor by her feet. The computer was right—a part from the device was lying there. "Oops."

She didn't want to admit it out loud, but it was time to consult the manual. As Ally reached across the dashboard to grab the tablet, her arm knocked into the juba juice. The bottle tipped, spilling sticky juice all over the manual and the dashboard.
The tablet sparked, while the dashboard fizzled and popped.
"Oh no!" Ally cried. "What have I done?"
"Sensors indicate you spilled juba juice, and the—"
"I know what I did!" Ally snapped. "I need to know how to undo it!"
The computer clicked, but Ally cut it off before it could speak. "No! Don't tell me! I'll figure it out myself. But first I'd better clean up this mess."

She hurried to get a towel. But somehow the toe of one of her boots got stuck on a rung of the chair. Ally lost her balance, and her hand slammed into the control lever. She gasped as she heard the escape pod's engine sparked to life. Then— whoosh! The pod started to zoom away from the mother ship.
"Alpha!" Ally shouted. "Stop this thing! Get me back to my parents' ship—fast!"
"Unable to comply. Escape pod is unable to redock with the mother ship at this time."
"What?" Ally blinked, trying to understand what she was hearing. "Then call my parents so I can ask them what to do!"
"Command does not compute. Communication device is offline."
"Oh no!" Ally cried, watching in horror as the pod hurtled into deep space.
The escape pod shot through space. Ally kept trying to turn it around, but nothing worked. Then suddenly things got worse.
"Warning: low fuel," the computer said.
"How low?" Ally snapped.
"Must land to refuel."
"Are you kidding me?" Ally groaned. "Where's the closest planet to refuel—and get parts to fix the comm device?"

The computer whirred. "Nearest planet with intelligent life is Earth. Atmosphere: oxygen. Dominant life-form: human, also called Earthling. Temperament: intelligent, creative, sometimes friendly but often dangerous. Previous attempts to make contact with humans: unsuccessful. Deemed too dangerous."
Ally gulped. "Dangerous?"
"Some humans are curious about visitors from other realms. But most are suspicious and respond with aggression."
"Yikes!" Ally had never heard of a life-form that didn't treat Astralians with deep respect.
"Engage meld medallion to activate human-shaped camouflage for protection."
"Phew!" Ally said. "I can camouflage myself to look like a human. Okay, Alpha, let's land on Earth."
Ally watched as the pod approached the pretty blue-and-green planet. "Earth matches my outfit," she thought. "It can't be too bad."

The pod flew low over a deserted sandy area before touching down behind some trees in a park. Ally slipped on her meld medallion, a necklace that contained special technology. It allowed her to blend in with other life-forms. She expected to feel different instantly, but instead she felt just like herself—until she looked in the mirror.
"Wow!" Her tentacles had been transformed into red, curly hair, and her nose was now sharp and pointy. But the most surprising change was to her feet.
"Ugh . . . My feet look so small now."
"Small feet are the least of your problems," the computer said.
Ally ignored the comment and went outside. She used her meld medallion to shrink the pod and camouflage it among the trees. "Don't go anywhere, Alpha. I might need to escape quickly from this place!"

As she stepped out from behind the trees, Ally saw some posters about local attractions along the path. Two humans—a mother and daughter—were looking at one of the posters. Ally tried to read their minds but couldn't hear anything.
"Hmm," she thought. "Maybe my mind-reading ability doesn't work here." She lifted her arms in a traditional Astralian greeting. "Hello!"
The little girl spun around. "An alien, Mommy! A real one!"
Ally froze.
But the mother smiled. "That's just a friendly teenager, honey. Wave and say hello!"
After the humans walked away, Ally went over to look at the posters. One showed a picture of a large glass building—with a GrayZonian spaceship floating above it.
Intrigued, Ally held up her meld medallion to translate the poster. It read, "Visit the World-Famous Sandville UFO Museum!"
"That sounds like the perfect place to find parts and fuel," Ally thought.

After walking around for thirty minutes, Ally still hadn't found the museum. She'd been on hot planets before, but this one seemed particularly warm with a blazing sun and no clouds. She felt hot and hungry.
Just then she caught a delicious scent. "Food!" She jumped up and followed the scent to a busy street with a crowded restaurant. A sign read, "Pepe's Diner. Grand Opening Today!"
Ally took a deep breath and went inside. To her relief, nobody looked at her in surprise. "Good!" she thought. "My meld medallion is working."
A waitress handed her a menu. "Only one seat is left at the counter."
Ally sat down and opened the menu. She wanted to use her meld medallion to translate it, but the waitress was watching her closely.
"I'll just have one of everything!" Ally blurted out.
"You got enough money? That'll cost hundreds of dollars."
"Dollars?" Ally shook her head. "I don't have any of those."
The waitress took the menu back. "Sorry, no handouts."
Ally was confused. "I didn't ask you for a hand . I asked for food ."
"If you want anything in this world, honey, you've got to work for it."

"Oh!" Ally finally understood. Unlike on other planets where food was free, Earthlings charged money for nourishment. "I can pay for my meal with good deeds. Do you have a war that you need stopped? Natural resources that need protection?"
"Ha-ha," the waitress said, but she wasn't laughing. "Like I said, you need to find a job."
"How?"
"Look for 'Help Wanted' signs."
Ally grinned. "No problem! Responding to cries for help is what we Astralians do best!" She leaped up and darted out the door.

"It will be easy to find someone to help," Ally thought as she walked through Sandville's downtown area. But Ally didn't spot any 'Help Wanted' signs. Nor did she pick up any cries for help. In fact, she saw hardly any humans on the street. Most of them were zooming by in vehicles.
Finally she spotted a man walking a four-legged animal with fluffy fur. She tried to read the man's thoughts but could pick up only a few words: "Milk . . . bread . . . dog biscuits."
It didn't sound like a cry for help, but Ally hurried toward him anyway. "Greetings! I am Allyzooba of Astralia. Can I be of help to you?"
The man scooped up his animal and backed away. Then he hurried off, muttering, "Kids these days are so weird!"
A little farther down the street, a woman stepped out of a store and headed to her vehicle. Ally tried to read her thoughts, but once again the words and images were fuzzy.

Ally sighed. Finding a human to help was going to be more challenging than she'd first thought. Especially since her Astral mind abilities weren't working well on this strange planet. But as she glimpsed her reflection in a large plate-glass window, something occurred to her. Her new human hair was long and thick.
"Hey!" she thought. "Maybe my hair is creating problems."
She tucked her hair behind her ears and listened again. This time a voice rang clearly in her head.
"I need help . . . I can't do everything myself."
Ally looked around. The cry was coming from the building right in front of her! She held up her meld medallion to read the sign on the window: Ray's Diner.
She hurried inside. Unlike Pepe's Diner, this one was almost empty. Three people in a booth were sipping hot beverages, and a man wearing a blue uniform and badge was sitting at the counter.
"I bet he's the one in charge," Ally thought.
"Greetings! Are you the commander here?" she asked.
The man looked up and laughed. "Me? I'm just a museum security guard. Ray's the one in charge around here." He pointed at a man working inside the kitchen.
Ally walked into the kitchen. "Greetings! I am Allyzooba of Astralia."
But there was so much noise from the grill and fan, the human named Ray didn't even turn around.
"Excuse me." Ally tapped him on the shoulder. "I am Allyzooba of Astralia. I have come to solve your woes, to do good deeds, and to spread great joy."
"You don't sound like you're from Australia!" Ray shouted over the noise.
"Not Australia—Astralia!" Ally shouted back. "And I have come to do—"
"Look, Ally." Ray wiped his brow. "Is it a job you want?"
She nodded.

"Well, I'll hire you," Ray said. "I need help because I can't cook, wash dishes, and wait on customers by myself. My son usually helps me, but he's busy this summer with soccer camp. And I'll be honest. I can't pay you much. You'll have to work for tips."
"You mean I can help you and get paid—in dollars?"
"It's not a lot, nothing to get excited about."
"Well, I'm really excited!" Ally exclaimed.
Ray smiled and grabbed an apron from a hook on the wall. He handed it to Ally, and she put it on. Then he went over to pick up a plate with a triple-decker sandwich. "Here. Take this."
"Thanks!" Ally licked her lips. She was about to take a bite when Ray shouted, "No! What are you doing? That's for Phil at the counter!"
"Oh! This is for a customer to eat!" Ally realized. She headed out of the kitchen with the plate. But on the way out, she tripped. "Whoa!"
The customers gasped as the sandwich slipped back and forth on the plate. Then, in the nick of time, Ally managed to catch her balance and save the sandwich.
"Hooray!" The customers clapped.

Ally smiled and took an Astralian bow. "Some earthlings are friendly, just as the computer said," she thought. But others, like the waitress at Pepe's and the man with the furry animal, had treated her rather meanly.
"No wonder humans also have a reputation for being dangerous," she thought. "They're so unpredictable!"
Plus, Earthlings had never made contact with an Astralian before. So while Ally was here on Earth, she would have to be careful—very careful.
After all the customers were gone, Ray handed Ally a sandwich.
"Who's this for?" she asked.
"You," Ray said. "You're not earning much money—the least I can do is feed you."
"Thanks!" Ally took a bite. "Delicious!"
Ray sighed. "Glad someone likes my food."
Just then a boy around Ally's age walked in. Ally was about to hand him a menu, but the boy smiled. "I'm not a customer. I'm Mateo, Ray's son."
"Hi, I'm Ally. I work here now."
"Welcome to Ray's," Mateo said. "Hey, Papi, how was business today?"
"Not so good," Ray replied. "Ally and I worked hard with just two of us. But that new place in town is stealing all my customers."
"People are just going to Pepe's because it's new," Mateo said.
"Good food should be what people care about," Ray muttered, as he went into the storeroom.
"He's right," Mateo said. "And I bet our food is better than Pepe's."
"The humans at Ray's are definitely better," Ally thought. Suddenly she spotted something familiar on Mateo's T-shirt. "Hey! Is that the OmegaDZed15 spaceship?"
Mateo shrugged. "It's a model ship from the UFO museum. What's the OmegaDZed whatever? I'm a space geek, but I've never heard of that."
"It's the Galorpians' star cruiser. They're a—"
"Ally!" Ray came out of the storeroom to tell her something. "I'm going to close up early. I'll understand if you don't want to come back tomorrow."
She blinked. "Did I do something wrong?"
"Not at all," Ray said. "But with so few customers, you couldn't have made much money today."
Ally had already counted her tips. "Is fifty dollars a lot?"
"Actually, that's not bad for a slow day," Mateo said. "The customers must have liked you."
"Come on, time to go home." Ray turned out the lights and led the way out of the diner.
Ally left the humans and returned to her ship, which was still hidden in the park. Once she was back inside, she slipped off her meld medallion.
The computer whirred to life as she sat down. "Scanning area, finding no new parts or fuel. Report."
"I need to earn more money," Ally said. "Calculate how much I need on this planet for new parts and fuel."
The computer clicked. "Calculating . . . $668.00."

Ally sighed. "It's going to take longer than I expected. But that's okay," she added, thinking of Ray. "Astralians are supposed to do lots of good deeds. Helping Ray will give me practice for real Astralian missions."
"Repeat warning!" The computer's lights flashed red. "Earthlings can be aggressive to beings from other planets! Use maximum caution!"
When Ally arrived at the diner the next day, Ray and Mateo were eating breakfast.
"You came back." Ray sounded surprised.
"Of course," Ally said.
"You sure you don't want me to stay and help today, Papi?" Mateo asked.
Ray shook his head. "Ally's here. Go have fun at soccer camp."
Mateo got up to leave, but he sat back down when two girls about his age walked in.
"Two bagels to go," one said without looking up from the comm device in her hand.
While Ally got their order ready, she noticed Mateo and the other girl smiling shyly at each other.
"Hmm," she thought. "Interesting." Was there an opportunity here for another good deed?
Ally quickly tucked her hair behind her ear. Then, as soon as the girls were gone, she turned to Mateo. "Do you know them?"
"Sort of. The one with the phone is Kate, and the . . . cute one is Bethany." Mateo blushed.
"Well, Bethany thinks you're cute too!"
Mateo laughed. "She does not!"
"She does!" Ally insisted. "I'm sure of it!"
Mateo got a dreamy look on his face and seemed to float out of the diner.
"I just made Mateo very happy!" Ally thought. Her parents might not think it was a big deal, but she felt very pleased.
Just then a customer walked in. She wore big glasses and had a beauty mark on her cheek. Ally hurried over.
"What do you recommend?" the woman asked.
"Ray's club sandwich is the best one in the universe," Ally replied. "Even better than the ones on Formaria12."
The woman looked confused. "Formaria12? Where's that restaurant?"
"Uh . . ." Ally gulped. "Nowhere. What would you like?"
The woman peered at Ally and then shrugged. "Well, if you say the sandwich is that good, then that's what I'll have."
"Phew!" Ally thought and hurried off to the kitchen. That had been a close call!
The next day when Ally got to work, Ray was in the office, punching numbers into a small machine.
Ally looked over his shoulder. "You made a mistake."
Ray glanced at a photo of a woman on the desk and sighed. "I've made more than one mistake."
"I mean your calculations. The total should be 9,789, not 7,989."
"Wow," Ray said. "You're good at math!" He entered the numbers into his machine again and then shook his head sadly. "You're also correct. Which means I'm even further in the red than I thought."
"What's wrong with red?" Ally asked. "It's one of my favorite colors! I mean, I look better in blue and purple, but . . ." Her words trailed off when Ray shook his head.
"'In the red' means you're losing money or not making a profit. It's bad news, Ally. I can't keep the diner open much longer."

Later Ally wiped down the counters, thinking hard. There had to be a way to help Ray save his diner. But she couldn't get money for Ray—she needed too much of it herself. Another problem was that she knew so little about how things worked on this planet.
"Wait a minute," she reminded herself. "You're an Astralian. And Astralians solve huge problems in the universe. There has to be a way to use your Astral mind to keep one tiny diner open."
Just then an old woman using a cane entered.
"I'll help you to a booth," Ally said.
"Aren't you sweet," the old woman said.
Ally got her settled and brought her a cup of tea. Next Phil, the museum security guard, came in.
"Coffee and an egg sandwich, over easy, with salsa and lettuce, right?" Ally asked.

"Yes!" Phil looked impressed. "You've only worked here for three days, and you remember my order. But I have to take it to go today. It's going to be busy at the museum. A local professor, Dr. Cosmo Lloyd, is giving a lecture on alien sightings."
Ally gulped. "Alien sightings?"
"Not real ones." Phil laughed. "Although some people think aliens are real. You know how the tourists and UFO fans are—they want to believe in life on other planets. I say it's all nonsense."
Ally forced a smile. "Crazy, right?"
"Oh, miss!" The old woman was waving to her. "I have a question."
Ally gave Phil's order to Ray and then went to the woman's table. "Yes?"
"I can't decide—scrambled eggs or pancakes. Which is better here?"
"They're both delicious. How about we give you half orders of each?"
"That sounds perfect!" the old woman said. "You've solved my problem!"
Ally gave a nervous laugh. "I've . . . um . . . got a special talent for solving problems."
That afternoon Mateo came in for lunch. He was wearing a T-shirt that Ally hadn't seen before.
"Nice shirt," she said.
"Thanks, it's one of my favorites. You can see all the details of Alpha Centauri."
"That's not Alpha Centauri," Ally said. "That's Beta Burgana."
"Beta Burgana?" Mateo laughed. "That sounds like the name of a fancy burger, doesn't it, Papi?"
"If we don't get more customers, there won't be any burgers," Ray grumbled.
"We'll think of a way to save the diner. Right, Ally?" Mateo said.
"Absolutely!" Ally sounded more confident than she felt.
When the old woman finished her meal, Ally helped her out the door. "Have a great day, and come back to see us again."
"Oh, I will!" The old woman winked. "I definitely will."
"Well, that's one more loyal customer," Ally thought.
A short while later, Bethany and Kate came in and sat down at the counter near Mateo.
Bethany grinned. "I have the same T-shirt."
"Really?" Mateo blushed. "Are you into science fiction too?"
"It's like all she ever thinks about," Kate said without looking away from her comm device.
Bethany laughed nervously. "Well, it's not the only thing."
Ally wasn't trying to read Bethany's mind, but the girl's thoughts suddenly blared in her ear. "That's right," Ally blurted out. "Bethany also thinks about Mateo all the time!"
"Oh my gosh!" Kate said.
Mateo and Bethany both turned bright red. Then Bethany grabbed Kate's hand and pulled her out of the diner.
"Ally!" Mateo shouted after the girls were gone. "I can't believe you said that!"
Ally blinked at him. "But it was true! And I was trying to do another good deed and help you!"
"Help me?" Mateo stared at her in disbelief. "That's not called help—it's called ruining everything!" He stormed out of the diner.
Early the next morning, the computer whirred to life. "Wake up. Time to report to work."
"I'm not going," Ally grumbled, and yanked the covers over her head.
"Irrational reply," the computer said. "Need fuel and new parts for travel to Astralia."
"I can't go back to the diner. Mateo hates me," Ally said.
"Irrational reply," the computer repeated. "An Astralian never gives up on a mission."
"Fine!" Ally got up and threw on her meld medallion. "I'll go find another job! Are you happy?"
"Irrational question," the computer replied.
Ally left the park and walked into town to look for a new job. But in order to get to some of the other businesses, she had to walk past Ray's.
"I'll just run," she thought. Then, as she got closer to the diner, she spotted Ray and Mateo out front. She ducked into a nearby alley.
"Mateo, I insist," Ray said. "You must go to camp today. The last few months have been hard enough on our family. I want you to have some fun."
"I don't want you to be lonely, Papi. Besides, if Ally has quit, it's all my fault."
"I doubt you're the reason she didn't show up today," Ray said. "With so few customers, she couldn't make enough money here. I'm sure she found a better-paying job."

Mateo sighed. "I shouldn't have yelled at her. Especially since I finally got up the nerve to text Bethany. Because of Ally, I invited Bethany to the sci-fi convention at the UFO museum next week, and she said yes!"
"That's great, son." Ray wrapped an arm around Mateo's shoulder and led him back inside.
Ally ran a hand through her hair. "Mateo's not mad at me anymore," she thought. "And Ray needs my help. Maybe . . ."
A minute later she strolled into the diner as if nothing had ever happened. "I'm sorry I'm late, I—"
"You're back," Ray said.
"I'm sorry I yelled at you, Ally," Mateo said. "I was just embarrassed in front of Bethany."
Ally waved her hand. "I've already forgotten about it. Don't you have a camp to get to, Mateo?"
"Yes," he said. "And thanks to you, I've also got a date with Bethany!"

Later in the day, customers began to trickle in. There was a family of four who ordered burgers, fries, and milkshakes. There was also a woman with bright red hair, rhinestone glasses, and a leopard-print dress.
Phil came running in. "Just a coffee to go. I've got to get back to the museum. There's a big alien-hunting crowd over there today."
"What?" Ally's stomach turned to knots. She tried to read Phil's mind, but all she could see was a doughnut.
"You know, a huge tour group," Phil said. "They come to the museum thinking they'll find proof of aliens and UFOs and try to track them down. Can you imagine?"
Ally gave a little laugh. "Nope!" Then she handed Phil his coffee and a doughnut. "Here, it's on the house."
"Chocolate! My favorite. How'd you know?" Phil asked.
She shrugged. "Lucky guess."
Ally put some of her tip money in the cash register to pay for Phil's doughnut. Then she went to serve the woman in the leopard-print dress. "Do you know what you'd like?"
"I wish I did." The woman stared at the menu.
"Let's see if I can help," Ally said.
She quickly scanned the woman's thoughts and saw a plate of eggs with spicy salsa. "How about Ray's huevos rancheros? That's two fried eggs on a crispy tortilla, salsa, and cheese."
The woman's face lit up. "That's exactly what I've been craving. I didn't see it on the menu, but you read my mind!"
Ten minutes later Ally was crossing the dining room with the woman's order and trying not to think about what Phil had said. It sounded like some humans actually hunted for aliens.
"I'm in more danger than I realized," Ally thought. She hadn't been looking where she was going. "Maybe I'd better—oops!"
As Ally slammed into an empty table, the plate of eggs flew up into the air. Instinctively Ally activated her levitating ability. The plate froze, floating in midair.
"Ack!" she thought. "I shouldn't have done that!"

Ally quickly grabbed the plate and looked around to see if anyone had spotted her trick. The woman in the leopard-print dress was looking right at her. When Ally met her eyes, the woman quickly looked away.

Ally delivered the huevos rancheros to the woman and then ducked into the kitchen, trying not to panic. But the customer had seen her levitation ability! And now the woman was typing rapidly into her comm device!
"What if she's one of those alien hunters?" Ally thought. "She might try to trap me and put me in the Sandville UFO Museum!"
Ally peeked out, watching the woman as she took a few bites of food and then put her fork down. She typed some more, casting her eyes all around the diner every once in a while.
Ally was trying to read the woman's mind when a couple entered the diner. Ally sighed and went out to greet them.
"Do you have room for us?" the woman asked.
Ally gestured around the nearly empty diner. "We sure do."
"Great!" the man said. "There are 12 of us."
Ally's eyes went wide. "Twelve?"
"We went to Pepe's first, but they said it would be a long wait."
"Oh! Well, sit wherever you like, and I'll be right back to take your orders."
Ally scurried to the office. "Ray!" she squealed. "Twelve people just walked in!"
When she returned to the dining room with water for the new customers, they were chattering away to one another.
". . . lecture on extraterrestrial life-forms . . ."
". . . the foremost authority on other galaxies . . ."
"No one knows more about the study of aliens . . ."

Then to Ally's horror, the woman in the leopard-print dress stood up and approached some people in the group.

She closed her eyes for a second, thinking about running away. But then her eyes landed on Ray, who was heating up a grill.

When Ally went to take the new customers' orders, the woman in the leopard-print dress was gone. Ally took a deep breath.
"What would you like?" she asked.
"I'll have huevos rancheros," the first diner said.
"Me too!"
"Me three!"

"Twelve orders of huevos rancheros coming right up!" She rushed to the kitchen.
Exactly one hour later, 12 satisfied customers filed out of the diner. None of them seemed to suspect a thing about Ally. And they all promised to come back with their friends and families soon.
Ally blew out a breath. "If even half of them come back," she murmured, "and bring about two people with them, and then those two people return and bring two more, that's—"

By the time Bethany and Kate arrived, Ally felt herself relaxing—just a little. The customer in the leopard-print dress had just been telling the other customers about Ray's good food. That was all.

They were finally gone, but Ally could still feel her heart pounding in her chest. She went over to the counter to refill some salt shakers, but she was so rattled, she spilled salt all over the place. She was cleaning it up when Ray called from the kitchen.

Ray's Diner, located near Sandville's famous UFO museum, is full of surprises. Though the decor is simple, there's nothing plain about the food or the service. Everything I ate there was delicious. Ally stood back, watching as the others started planning the restaurant makeover. She was happy that Ray's Diner might be saved after all. But now she herself needed help.

Late in the afternoon, things were quiet enough for Ally to take a break.

As Ally walked along, she stopped and looked around. "I'm going to miss it here," she thought. "And I need to remember everything so I can tell my parents about Earth. After all, I am the first Astralian to make contact with Earthlings."

The Sandville UFO Museum was a tall glass building with banners displaying planets and stars. As soon as Ally stepped through the door, an alarm blared.

Barry followed Ally around for the first part of her shift as she waited on customers. After a couple of hours, she handed him his own apron and pad.
